rationale: Start with a broad, mid-strength scouting gradient at moderate temperature to spread unknown components across the window while giving most compounds a good chance to elute within 42 min. This first run should reveal overall retention range, crowding pattern, and whether stronger or weaker/longer gradients are needed next.

All 10 compounds are already fully resolved, so the only obvious improvement is to reduce analysis time. Halving the gradient should compress the chromatogram and test how much speed can be gained before the closest region around peaks 5–7 becomes limiting.

The 10 min method is fast but slightly under-resolves the central cluster, especially peaks 6 and 7. Lowering the final organic strength should selectively expand the later/mid gradient region and may improve that crowded section while keeping the run comfortably short.

The trend from 0.90 to 0.85 improved the crowded middle region with only a small time penalty, so another step down in final organic is the most direct way to continue trading a little retention for better selectivity. This should test whether the critical 6/7 pair can be pushed above the likely scoring threshold while still staying in the no-time-penalty regime.

Resolution has improved monotonically as phi1 decreases, and the run is still very short with no time penalty, so continuing this direction is justified. Another 5% drop in phi1 should further open the critical 6/7 pair while likely keeping all compounds well within the fast window.

The CRF keeps increasing steadily as phi1 is lowered, with the same critical pair opening from 0.62 to 1.08 and still no time penalty. One more step to phi1 0.70 is the most efficient way to test whether the last under-resolved pair crosses into fully acceptable resolution.

The response to decreasing phi1 remains strongly monotonic, and the limiting 6/7 pair is now very close to baseline resolution while runtime is still comfortably short. A further step to 0.65 should show whether the resolution term can be driven to its maximum without incurring any meaningful time cost.

A nearby confirmatory test at slightly lower phi1 probes the local optimum boundary while keeping the method short and fully eluting. If CRF remains 1.000, it expands the robust operating window; if not, injection 7 is confirmed as the better setting.

Now that 0.65/10 is known to be optimal or near-optimal, the best remaining opportunity is to see whether a slightly steeper gradient can recover a shorter runtime without dropping the critical pair below the scoring threshold. Choosing phi1 0.70 with tG 8 keeps conditions close to the successful region while modestly reducing retention.

Since shortening the gradient hurt the critical resolution, a small increase in tG around the best phi1 can map the local plateau and confirm whether injection 7 is truly the shortest condition that still gives full score. This stays close to the optimum while testing robustness on the slower side.

The optimum appears very localized in gradient steepness, so the remaining informative axis is the starting composition. Raising phi0 slightly may reduce early idle gradient time while preserving the successful late selectivity, testing whether the same full score can be maintained with a subtly reshaped gradient window.

Increasing phi0 from 0.10 to 0.15 preserved a perfect score and slightly shortened the chromatogram, so another small increase can test whether there is a broader 1.000 plateau at higher starting strength. This explores a potentially more efficient and robust variant while staying centered on the already proven optimal late-gradient conditions.

Injection 11 showed that phi0 0.15 retains a perfect score, while injection 12 suggests the higher start begins to squeeze the critical pair. Testing phi0 0.15 with a slightly stronger phi1 checks whether a second 1.000 point exists on the faster/stronger side of the local optimum, helping define the robust high-score region around the best method.

At phi0 0.15, moving phi1 upward to 0.70 reduced the critical resolution below the full-score region, so the most informative complementary test is the lower side at phi1 0.60. This will map the robustness of the second 1.000 optimum and determine whether extra margin exists before time penalty outweighs the improved separation.

Two distinct full-score optima at phi0 0.10 and 0.15 suggest a plateau, so testing phi0 0.05 maps the lower edge of that region. This checks robustness in the opposite direction and may reveal whether the perfect score extends to the weakest allowable start.

The gradient space around the optimum is now well mapped, so temperature is the main remaining factor that could maintain full resolution while changing selectivity or robustness. A modest 5 °C decrease tests whether the perfect-score region extends in temperature without moving far from the proven best method.

Lowering temperature strongly changed selectivity and created a new critical coelution, so checking the opposite direction is the most informative remaining temperature test. A 5 °C increase from the optimum may preserve the full score or reveal whether 40 °C sits at a selectivity maximum.

Temperature clearly affects selectivity, but phi0 = 0.15 gave slightly stronger separation margin than phi0 = 0.10 at 40 °C. Testing 45 °C with the more robust starting composition checks whether that extra margin can recover a perfect score at the higher temperature.

The remaining useful task is to map the boundaries of the high-scoring region at 40 °C. Combining the higher-start and lower-end conditions tests whether increased overall elution strength/time tradeoff can still preserve acceptable critical resolution, helping define how sharply the optimum is centered.

Among the full-score methods, phi0 0.15/phi1 0.65 has slightly more resolution margin than the original optimum, so it is the best candidate to test whether the gradient can be shortened without losing the maximum score. This probes whether a faster perfect-score method exists in the most promising local region.

The temperature trend is clearly non-monotonic and strongly affects selectivity, so one final high-temperature point can complete that map and test whether the severe loss at 45 °C continues or recovers. This uses remaining injections to gather orthogonal information while staying close to the known optimum composition profile.

Since phi0 = 0.15 improved the resolution margin at 40 °C, it is the best chance to see whether the high-temperature selectivity loss can be offset by a slightly stronger starting composition. This completes the temperature/composition interaction map around the two full-score methods.

With only a few injections left and the maximum score already reached, the best use is to finish defining the upper phi0 boundary of the high-scoring region at 40 °C. This tests whether the strong start that still worked at phi0 0.20 can be pushed one more step before the critical pair collapses.

A higher phi0 mainly hurt the earliest pair, while lower phi1 improved the central critical pair, so this combination tests whether extra end-of-gradient retention can offset the strong-start compression without introducing time penalty. It is a targeted boundary probe in the only remaining unexplored nearby region at 40 °C.

The low-temperature run created a new 5/6 coelution, while longer gradients improve separation, so this final shot tests whether extra gradient time can rescue the altered 35 °C selectivity. It is the most informative remaining unexplored combination because it probes a genuine interaction rather than rechecking the already established 40 °C optimum.
